metadata.title: INFECTIOUS DISEASES OSCE
metadata.subtitle: 15 Structured Stations
metadata.audienceAndScoring: Final-Year MBBS • 8 minutes per station • 20-point analytic checklist
metadata.includedMaterials: Candidate materials • Standardised scripts • Examiner guides • Learning notes
facultyNote: Built in the same station architecture as the preceding OSCE manuals. All patient names in source-derived scenarios have been changed.

The uploaded notes are used as the scenario base for typhoid, malaria, dengue, rabies and varicella/rubella-related encounters. Several treatment details in the notes are historical or locally specific; drug choice, dose, prophylaxis schedules, isolation and referral pathways must be checked against current institutional/provincial/national guidance before summative use.
Additional high-yield stations are included to broaden KMU MBBS and CPSP-style clinical coverage: sepsis, PUO, cholera, tetanus, meningitis, pulmonary TB and HIV testing/counselling.

The focus is clinical reasoning, infection prevention, appropriate investigations, recognition of danger signs, escalation, counselling and safe management rather than memorisation of a single drug regimen.
assessmentDesign: Each station uses 10 observable criteria scored 0–2 (20 marks).
Critical safety errors may justify an overall fail despite the analytic score.
Local policy supersedes this teaching document.
contents: 4. Severe Dengue / Dengue Shock Data Interpretation
15. Fever in Returning Traveller — Integrated Data Interpretation

stations.title: Typhoid Fever
stations.primaryCompetency: Focused infectious-disease history, examination plan and management
candidateInstructions: Mr. Adeel Rahman, 31, has 3 weeks of fever, malaise, headache and abdominal symptoms after working in an area with unsafe food and water.
Take a focused history, state the relevant examination, propose investigations and explain your initial management.
candidateHandout: Clarify exposure to unsafe food/water, duration/pattern of fever, bowel symptoms, abdominal pain and complications.
Do not rely on a single serological screening test when cultures are available.
simulationScript: Fever 3 weeks; poor appetite; initially constipated, now loose stools and abdominal discomfort.
Recently worked in a rural settlement and ate from street vendors; drinking-water hygiene was poor.
Examiner findings if requested: febrile, relative bradycardia, faint blanching truncal macules, soft splenomegaly.
examinerInstructions: Allow the candidate to proceed without coaching.
If a required datum is not obtainable by simulation, provide it only when the candidate asks appropriately.
Award prompted checklist items no more than 1/2. Prioritise safe recognition, escalation and infection-control behaviour.
keyAnswerGuide: Likely enteric (typhoid) fever.
Obtain blood cultures ideally before antibiotics; CBC/LFTs and stool culture as clinically appropriate.
Assess hydration and complications such as GI bleeding/perforation, encephalopathy or shock.
Antibiotic selection must reflect current local resistance/antibiogram and severity; escalate/admit if toxic or complicated.
Food/water hygiene and follow-up are essential.
suggestedApproach: Establish exposure and time course.
Characterise fever and GI symptoms.
Look for red flags/complications.
Examine vitals, hydration, abdomen, rash and spleen.
Culture before treatment where feasible; treat according to current local protocol.

checklist.criterion: Introduces self, confirms identity/consent and uses infection-control precautions.
Elicits unsafe food/water exposure and duration/pattern of fever.
Asks bowel symptoms, abdominal pain, appetite, headache and constitutional symptoms.
Screens GI bleeding/perforation, altered mental state and shock.
States focused vitals, hydration, abdominal, skin and splenic examination.
Prioritises blood culture and appropriate baseline laboratory tests.
Recognises likely enteric fever and gives sensible differentials.
Explains supportive care and antimicrobial treatment guided by current resistance/local protocol.
Provides hygiene/transmission advice and safety-netting.
Summarises, checks understanding and arranges review/escalation.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring anchor: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/unsafe/incorrect. Prompted items score a maximum of 1/2.
promptQuestions: What is the most useful microbiological test early in illness?
Name two serious complications of enteric fever.
criticalSafetyErrors: Failure to recognise shock, GI bleeding/perforation or encephalopathy.
Prescribing from an outdated fixed regimen without considering resistance or local policy.
sourceNote: Source-derived scenario: uploaded infectious-disease notes, typhoid section; patient name changed. Management deliberately updated to require current local antimicrobial guidance.

stations.title: Malaria
stations.primaryCompetency: Travel fever history, diagnosis and severity assessment
candidateInstructions: Mr. Haris Khan, 34, presents with recurrent fever, rigors, sweats and severe headache after travel to a malaria-endemic area.
Take a focused history and explain investigations and initial management.
candidateHandout: Always assess severity: altered consciousness, hypoglycaemia, jaundice, renal impairment, severe anaemia, respiratory distress or shock.
Species and local resistance influence definitive therapy.
simulationScript: Episodes of fever with rigors and drenching sweats; myalgia and headache.
Recent travel to an endemic rural area; no prophylaxis.
If asked: dark urine and increasing lethargy today.
examinerInstructions: Allow the candidate to proceed without coaching.
If a required datum is not obtainable by simulation, provide it only when the candidate asks appropriately.
Award prompted checklist items no more than 1/2. Prioritise safe recognition, escalation and infection-control behaviour.
keyAnswerGuide: Malaria is a medical priority in a febrile returning traveller.
Thick and thin blood films and/or validated rapid diagnostic testing; repeat testing if suspicion remains high despite an initial negative test.
CBC, glucose, renal/liver profile and severity assessment.
Severe malaria requires urgent admission and parenteral therapy per current national/WHO/local protocol.
suggestedApproach: Travel/exposure → fever pattern → severity → differentials → malaria testing → supportive/definitive management.

checklist.criterion: Introduces self and clarifies travel geography/dates.
Characterises fever, rigors, sweats and interval symptoms.
Asks prophylaxis and mosquito exposure.
Screens altered consciousness, seizures, dyspnoea, jaundice, oliguria, bleeding and shock.
States focused vitals, GCS, hydration and abdominal/splenic examination.
Requests thick/thin film or validated malaria test and baseline labs including glucose.
Recognises severe features and need for admission if present.
Explains treatment is species/severity/resistance dependent and follows current protocol.
Gives mosquito-bite prevention/travel advice.
Safety-nets and arranges urgent escalation/review.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring anchor: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/unsafe/incorrect. Prompted items score a maximum of 1/2.
promptQuestions: What makes malaria severe?
What should you do if the first film is negative but suspicion remains high?
criticalSafetyErrors: Missing cerebral malaria/hypoglycaemia/shock.
Delaying urgent treatment in severe malaria.
sourceNote: Source-derived from uploaded malaria scenario; patient name changed. Exact antimalarial regimens in the source are historical and are not reproduced as fixed prescriptions.

stations.title: Dengue Fever
stations.primaryCompetency: Focused assessment, warning signs and counselling
candidateInstructions: Ms. Mehwish Tariq, 27, has 4 days of fever, severe myalgia, retro-orbital pain and a rash.
Assess her for dengue, identify warning signs, request appropriate tests and counsel her.
candidateHandout: The key OSCE task is not just naming dengue: identify warning signs and the critical phase, hydration status, bleeding and shock.
Avoid aspirin/NSAIDs where dengue is suspected.
simulationScript: High fever, severe body aches, retro-orbital pain, nausea and macular rash.
No major bleeding yet. On day 4 she has increasing abdominal discomfort.
examinerInstructions: Allow the candidate to proceed without coaching.
If a required datum is not obtainable by simulation, provide it only when the candidate asks appropriately.
Award prompted checklist items no more than 1/2. Prioritise safe recognition, escalation and infection-control behaviour.
keyAnswerGuide: Likely dengue. CBC with serial haematocrit/platelets; dengue testing depends on illness day and local diagnostic pathway.
Warning signs include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy/restlessness, fluid accumulation, hepatomegaly and rising haematocrit with falling platelets.
Supportive care and careful fluids; paracetamol for fever/pain; avoid NSAIDs/aspirin.
Escalate/admit when warning signs, shock, inability to maintain oral intake, significant bleeding or high-risk comorbidity are present.
suggestedApproach: Confirm day of illness and epidemiology.
Assess warning signs and haemodynamics.
Order appropriate serial labs.
Explain hydration, safe antipyresis and return precautions.

checklist.criterion: Introduces self and establishes day of illness/exposure.
Elicits fever, retro-orbital pain, myalgia/arthralgia, rash and GI symptoms.
Screens bleeding and all major warning signs.
Assesses oral intake, urine output and dehydration.
States vitals including pulse pressure, perfusion and abdominal examination.
Requests CBC with serial haematocrit/platelets and appropriate dengue testing.
Explains supportive care and careful hydration.
Avoids aspirin/NSAIDs and uses safe antipyretic advice.
Recognises indications for admission/escalation.
Provides mosquito-control advice and clear safety-netting.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring anchor: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/unsafe/incorrect. Prompted items score a maximum of 1/2.
promptQuestions: Why is pulse pressure important?
What laboratory trend suggests plasma leakage?
criticalSafetyErrors: Giving aspirin/NSAIDs.
Missing shock or warning signs.
sourceNote: Source-derived from uploaded dengue material; patient name changed. Current institutional dengue pathways should determine testing and fluid prescriptions.

stations.title: Severe Dengue / Dengue Shock Data Interpretation
stations.primaryCompetency: Interpretation of trends and emergency escalation
candidateInstructions: Review the observation chart and laboratory trend supplied by the examiner for Ms. Anum Shah, 22, with suspected dengue.
Interpret the data, state the likely complication and outline immediate priorities.
candidateHandout: Data: Day 3 Hct 36%, platelets 120×10⁹/L. Day 5 Hct 45%, platelets 58×10⁹/L. BP 90/76, pulse 118, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 s, urine output falling.
simulationScript: No additional history unless asked.
examinerInstructions: Allow the candidate to proceed without coaching.
If a required datum is not obtainable by simulation, provide it only when the candidate asks appropriately.
Award prompted checklist items no more than 1/2. Prioritise safe recognition, escalation and infection-control behaviour.
keyAnswerGuide: Rising haematocrit plus falling platelets and narrowing pulse pressure with poor perfusion suggests plasma leakage with dengue shock.
Immediate ABC assessment, monitored IV access, judicious isotonic crystalloid according to current dengue shock protocol, frequent reassessment and senior/critical-care escalation.
Look for bleeding; avoid reflex platelet transfusion based only on count.
suggestedApproach: Recognise shock → ABC → access/monitoring → fluid resuscitation per protocol → repeat Hct/clinical response → search for bleeding/organ dysfunction.

checklist.criterion: Correctly identifies rising haematocrit and falling platelets.
Calculates/recognises narrow pulse pressure.
Recognises shock/critical phase rather than “improving fever”.
Calls for urgent ABC assessment and senior help.
Requests monitored IV access and appropriate crystalloid resuscitation per protocol.
Plans frequent reassessment of BP, pulse pressure, capillary refill and mental state.
Monitors urine output and repeat haematocrit.
Assesses for occult/overt bleeding and organ dysfunction.
Avoids unnecessary NSAIDs/IM injections and non-indicated platelet transfusion.
Communicates urgency and safe escalation clearly.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring anchor: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/unsafe/incorrect. Prompted items score a maximum of 1/2.
promptQuestions: What would a falling haematocrit in a shocked patient make you consider?
Why can excessive fluids be dangerous in dengue?
criticalSafetyErrors: Failure to recognise shock.
Large unmonitored fluid administration without reassessment.
sourceNote: Source-derived from the uploaded DHF/critical-phase material; converted into a high-yield interpretation station.

stations.title: Rabies Post-Exposure Prophylaxis
stations.primaryCompetency: Animal-bite assessment, wound care and PEP counselling
candidateInstructions: Ms. Zoya Malik, 36, was bitten on the hand 2 hours ago by an unprovoked stray dog that cannot be traced.
Take a focused history, assess the wound and explain immediate management.
candidateHandout: Do not delay wound washing or indicated PEP while waiting for symptoms.
Use current national/WHO-approved vaccine and rabies immunoglobulin schedules.
simulationScript: Unprovoked stray-dog bite; dog ran away.
No prior rabies vaccination. Tetanus status uncertain.
Wound: broken skin with bleeding on hand; distal neurovascular status intact.
examinerInstructions: Allow the candidate to proceed without coaching.
If a required datum is not obtainable by simulation, provide it only when the candidate asks appropriately.
Award prompted checklist items no more than 1/2. Prioritise safe recognition, escalation and infection-control behaviour.
keyAnswerGuide: Immediate thorough washing/irrigation with soap and water; appropriate antisepsis and wound assessment.

Classify exposure and give rabies vaccine; for severe transdermal exposure in an unvaccinated patient, infiltrate rabies immunoglobulin into/around wounds as anatomically feasible according to current protocol.
Assess tetanus prophylaxis and antibiotic need based on wound risk.
suggestedApproach: Exposure details → wound/host risk → irrigation → rabies PEP → tetanus/antibiotic assessment → follow-up.

checklist.criterion: Clarifies time, animal, provocation, traceability and bite site.
Asks prior rabies vaccination and tetanus status.
Assesses immunocompromise and wound contamination.
Examines depth, tissue/tendon/joint involvement and neurovascular status.
Initiates immediate copious soap-and-water irrigation.
Correctly identifies high-risk transdermal exposure.
Recommends vaccine promptly using current approved schedule.
Recommends RIG infiltration into/around wounds when indicated, per current protocol.
Addresses tetanus and selective antibiotic prophylaxis.
Gives follow-up, adherence and urgent-return advice.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring anchor: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/unsafe/incorrect. Prompted items score a maximum of 1/2.
promptQuestions: Should PEP wait for symptoms?
Where should rabies immunoglobulin be administered?
criticalSafetyErrors: Delaying PEP in a high-risk exposure.
Giving RIG only at a distant IM site rather than infiltrating wounds when indicated.
sourceNote: Source-derived from uploaded rabies dog-bite scenario; patient name changed. Historical vaccine/RIG details in the source are intentionally replaced by “current approved protocol”.

stations.title: Chickenpox Exposure in Pregnancy
stations.primaryCompetency: Risk assessment and counselling after varicella exposure
candidateInstructions: Ms. Eman Raza, 28, is 18 weeks pregnant and had significant household exposure to chickenpox yesterday. She is unsure whether she had chickenpox as a child.
Assess risk and counsel her on next steps.
candidateHandout: This is a counselling/risk-stratification station.
Exact prophylaxis depends on immune status, timing and current obstetric/infectious-disease guidance.
simulationScript: Well at present; no rash or fever.
No reliable history of prior varicella infection or vaccination.
examinerInstructions: Allow the candidate to proceed without coaching.
If a required datum is not obtainable by simulation, provide it only when the candidate asks appropriately.
Award prompted checklist items no more than 1/2. Prioritise safe recognition, escalation and infection-control behaviour.
keyAnswerGuide: Confirm significant exposure and maternal immunity with appropriate serology if uncertain.
If susceptible, arrange time-sensitive post-exposure prophylaxis according to current local obstetric/infectious-disease guidance.
Explain maternal pneumonia risk and fetal/neonatal implications without alarmist language.
If rash develops, isolate from vulnerable contacts and seek urgent review for respiratory/neurological symptoms.
suggestedApproach: Exposure → immunity → gestation → prophylaxis pathway → warning signs → obstetric follow-up.

checklist.criterion: Clarifies exposure timing/intensity and gestational age.
Asks prior chickenpox/vaccine history.
Checks immunosuppression/comorbidity and current symptoms.
Explains need to establish immunity if uncertain.
Recognises susceptible pregnancy as higher risk.
Arranges timely prophylaxis/specialist advice per current protocol.
Explains maternal and fetal risks proportionately.
Gives isolation advice if infection develops.
Safety-nets chest symptoms, neurological symptoms, severe rash/bleeding.
Arranges obstetric/infectious-disease follow-up and checks understanding.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring anchor: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/unsafe/incorrect. Prompted items score a maximum of 1/2.
promptQuestions: Why is immunity status important?
Name two maternal red flags requiring urgent hospital assessment.
criticalSafetyErrors: Giving a live varicella vaccine during pregnancy.
Failing to arrange time-sensitive prophylaxis/specialist advice in a susceptible pregnant patient.
sourceNote: Source-derived from uploaded chickenpox-in-pregnancy material; patient name changed. Prophylaxis timing/product must follow current local guidance.

stations.title: Rubella Exposure in Pregnancy
stations.primaryCompetency: Exposure history, investigation and non-directive counselling
candidateInstructions: Ms. Hiba Noor, 25, is 10 weeks pregnant and reports close contact with a child who later developed a rubella-like illness.
Take a focused history and explain investigations and counselling.
candidateHandout: Do not make irreversible recommendations from exposure history alone. Confirm diagnosis/immunity and involve obstetric/fetal-medicine services.
simulationScript: No current symptoms. Unsure of vaccination history.
Very anxious about fetal effects.
examinerInstructions: Allow the candidate to proceed without coaching.
If a required datum is not obtainable by simulation, provide it only when the candidate asks appropriately.
Award prompted checklist items no more than 1/2. Prioritise safe recognition, escalation and infection-control behaviour.
keyAnswerGuide: Clarify exposure and maternal symptoms; check documented immunity/vaccination.
Arrange appropriate rubella serology/testing with specialist interpretation; consider alternative rash illnesses as appropriate.
If maternal infection is confirmed early in pregnancy, provide specialist fetal-risk counselling and discuss options non-directively.
MMR is not given during pregnancy; susceptible women should be offered postpartum vaccination per policy.
suggestedApproach: Exposure → immunity → testing → specialist confirmation → balanced counselling → postpartum prevention.

checklist.criterion: Clarifies timing and nature of exposure.
Asks rash, fever, arthralgia and lymphadenopathy symptoms.
Checks vaccination/documented immunity.
Explains testing rather than assuming infection.
Requests appropriate rubella serology/testing with specialist interpretation.
Recognises early pregnancy as the highest fetal-risk period if infection is confirmed.
Uses non-directive, non-stigmatising counselling.
Refers to obstetric/fetal-medicine/infectious-disease team.
Avoids live MMR during pregnancy and discusses postpartum vaccination if nonimmune.
Addresses anxiety, checks understanding and arranges follow-up.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring anchor: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/unsafe/incorrect. Prompted items score a maximum of 1/2.
promptQuestions: What classic lymph nodes may enlarge in rubella?
Can MMR be given during pregnancy?
criticalSafetyErrors: Recommending termination solely from an unconfirmed exposure.
Administering live MMR during pregnancy.
sourceNote: Source-derived from uploaded rubella-and-pregnancy section; converted to a safer contemporary counselling station.

stations.title: Sepsis — Early Recognition & Initial Management
stations.primaryCompetency: Recognition and immediate resuscitation of suspected sepsis
candidateInstructions: Mr. Sameer Iqbal, 62, presents with fever, confusion, productive cough and hypotension.
Perform an initial assessment and tell the examiner your immediate management priorities.
candidateHandout: Observations: T 39.1°C, HR 124, BP 84/52, RR 30, SpO₂ 90% room air, confused.
simulationScript: History may reveal 2 days of cough and rigors.
Examiner provides findings only when requested.
examinerInstructions: Allow the candidate to proceed without coaching.
If a required datum is not obtainable by simulation, provide it only when the candidate asks appropriately.
Award prompted checklist items no more than 1/2. Prioritise safe recognition, escalation and infection-control behaviour.
keyAnswerGuide: Suspected infection with shock and organ dysfunction: treat as sepsis/septic shock.

ABC resuscitation, oxygen as indicated, IV access, lactate/bloods and cultures without delaying treatment, prompt empiric IV antimicrobials per local sepsis policy, judicious crystalloid with reassessment, urine output monitoring and urgent senior/critical-care escalation.
suggestedApproach: Recognise → call for help → ABC → access/investigations/cultures → antibiotics → fluids/reassessment → source control/ICU.

checklist.criterion: Recognises sepsis with shock and calls for urgent senior help.
Uses ABCDE and appropriate oxygen/monitoring.
Obtains IV access and requests lactate, CBC, renal/liver profile and other indicated tests.
Obtains blood cultures before antibiotics if this causes no meaningful delay.
Starts prompt empiric IV antimicrobials according to local source/sepsis guideline.
Gives appropriate crystalloid resuscitation with frequent reassessment.
Monitors urine output and mental state.
Considers source identification/control and chest imaging/urine testing as indicated.
Escalates persistent hypotension for vasopressor/critical-care support.
Communicates clearly and documents time-critical interventions.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring anchor: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/unsafe/incorrect. Prompted items score a maximum of 1/2.
promptQuestions: What bedside marker can help assess tissue hypoperfusion?
What if hypotension persists after appropriate fluids?
criticalSafetyErrors: Delaying antibiotics in septic shock.
Failure to escalate persistent hypotension/organ dysfunction.
sourceNote: Added high-yield station. KMU infectious-disease curriculum explicitly includes sepsis with OSPE/OSCE practical performance and initial management.

stations.title: Pyrexia of Unknown Origin
stations.primaryCompetency: Structured fever history and investigation planning
candidateInstructions: Ms. Ayesha Gul, 41, has recurrent documented fever for several weeks with no diagnosis after initial assessment.
Take a structured history and outline your examination and investigation strategy.
candidateHandout: Use broad categories: infection, malignancy, inflammatory/autoimmune and miscellaneous/drug-related causes.
simulationScript: Fever 4 weeks; fatigue and 3-kg weight loss.
No diagnosis from initial basic tests. Further details only if asked.
examinerInstructions: Allow the candidate to proceed without coaching.
If a required datum is not obtainable by simulation, provide it only when the candidate asks appropriately.
Award prompted checklist items no more than 1/2. Prioritise safe recognition, escalation and infection-control behaviour.
keyAnswerGuide: Reconfirm true fever and chronology; exposures/travel, TB contact, animals, procedures/devices, drugs, immune status and focal symptoms.
Full examination including skin, nodes, heart, abdomen, joints and fundi where appropriate.
Investigations should be hypothesis-driven: repeat basic labs/cultures and targeted imaging/serology rather than indiscriminate panels.
suggestedApproach: Confirm fever → exposure map → systems review → drugs/immune status → full exam → staged tests.

checklist.criterion: Establishes duration/pattern and documents true fever.
Asks travel, TB contact, animal/food/water and occupational exposures.
Asks procedures, prosthetic material, IV drug use and dental history where relevant.
Performs broad systems review including weight loss/night sweats.
Reviews drugs and immunosuppression.
States comprehensive physical examination including nodes, skin, heart and abdomen.
Requests rational baseline labs and cultures.
Uses targeted imaging/serology guided by clues.
Considers infectious, malignant, inflammatory and miscellaneous causes.
Avoids premature empiric therapy in a stable undiagnosed patient and plans review/escalation.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring anchor: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/unsafe/incorrect. Prompted items score a maximum of 1/2.
promptQuestions: Name four broad categories of PUO causes.
Why can indiscriminate testing be unhelpful?
criticalSafetyErrors: Missing immunosuppression or TB/endocarditis clues.
Unfocused empiric antibiotics in a stable patient without a diagnostic plan.
sourceNote: Added high-yield station. KMU infectious-disease curriculum includes fever and pyrexia of unknown origin.

stations.title: Acute Watery Diarrhoea / Cholera
candidateInstructions: Mr. Waqas Ali, 38, presents with sudden profuse watery diarrhoea after attending a large gathering.
Assess severity and explain immediate management and public-health priorities.
candidateHandout: The key skill is rapid dehydration/shock assessment and safe rehydration.
simulationScript: Large-volume painless watery stools and vomiting for 12 hours.
Very thirsty; reduced urine. Several attendees are also unwell.
examinerInstructions: Allow the candidate to proceed without coaching.
If a required datum is not obtainable by simulation, provide it only when the candidate asks appropriately.
Award prompted checklist items no more than 1/2. Prioritise safe recognition, escalation and infection-control behaviour.
keyAnswerGuide: Assess dehydration/shock immediately.
ORS for patients able to drink; IV isotonic rehydration for severe dehydration/shock according to current cholera/acute diarrhoea protocol, then replace ongoing losses.
Send stool testing when indicated/outbreak setting; antibiotics only when indicated and per local susceptibility policy.
Contact precautions, safe water/sanitation and public-health notification/outbreak control.
suggestedApproach: ABCDE → dehydration → rehydration → electrolytes/glucose → stool/public health → selective antibiotics.

checklist.criterion: Elicits stool frequency/volume, vomiting and duration.
Asks urine output, thirst, dizziness and ability to drink.
Screens blood in stool, fever and severe abdominal pain.
Assesses vitals, perfusion, mucosa, skin turgor and mental state.
Recognises severe dehydration/shock when present.
Starts appropriate oral or IV rehydration according to severity.
Plans electrolyte/glucose/renal assessment and replacement of ongoing losses.
Requests stool testing when clinically/public-health indicated.
Uses antibiotics selectively according to current protocol/resistance.
Addresses infection control, safe water/sanitation and outbreak notification.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring anchor: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/unsafe/incorrect. Prompted items score a maximum of 1/2.
promptQuestions: What is the immediate lifesaving treatment in cholera?
When is IV fluid required?
criticalSafetyErrors: Delaying rehydration while awaiting stool results.
Failure to recognise shock.
sourceNote: Added high-yield station. KMU infectious-disease course content includes cholera and practical management of GIT infection.

stations.title: Tetanus — Recognition & Initial Management
stations.primaryCompetency: Recognition, airway safety and toxin-control strategy
candidateInstructions: Mr. Daniyal Shah, 47, develops trismus and painful generalized spasms one week after a contaminated puncture wound.
State your focused assessment and immediate management priorities.
candidateHandout: Minimise unnecessary stimulation; airway compromise and autonomic instability can be life-threatening.
simulationScript: No reliable vaccination record.
Wound was not medically treated.
examinerInstructions: Allow the candidate to proceed without coaching.
If a required datum is not obtainable by simulation, provide it only when the candidate asks appropriately.
Award prompted checklist items no more than 1/2. Prioritise safe recognition, escalation and infection-control behaviour.
keyAnswerGuide: Clinical diagnosis. Urgent monitored admission/ICU assessment.
Airway/ventilation readiness; reduce stimuli; control spasms per protocol.
Wound cleaning/debridement, tetanus immune globulin according to current protocol, appropriate antimicrobial therapy and active vaccination because disease does not confer reliable immunity.
suggestedApproach: Recognise → quiet monitored environment → airway → neutralise unbound toxin → eradicate source → spasm/autonomic control → vaccination.

checklist.criterion: Recognises tetanus from trismus/spasms plus wound history.
Checks airway/breathing and calls for urgent senior/ICU help.
Minimises stimulation and monitors autonomic instability.
Assesses wound and vaccination history.
Plans wound cleaning/debridement.
Recommends tetanus immune globulin per current protocol.
Recommends appropriate antimicrobial therapy per protocol.
Plans spasm control and ventilatory support if needed.
Starts/continues active tetanus vaccination.
Explains prognosis, prevention and follow-up.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring anchor: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/unsafe/incorrect. Prompted items score a maximum of 1/2.
promptQuestions: Does tetanus infection itself provide reliable immunity?
What two immediate complications can kill the patient?
criticalSafetyErrors: Failure to secure/escalate airway risk.
Omitting immune globulin or active vaccination when indicated.
sourceNote: Added high-yield station. KMU infectious-disease curriculum includes tetanus and practical management.

stations.title: Acute Bacterial Meningitis
stations.primaryCompetency: Emergency recognition, investigations and empiric treatment
candidateInstructions: Ms. Laiba Ahmed, 20, presents with fever, severe headache, neck stiffness and increasing drowsiness.
Assess her and state your immediate management.
candidateHandout: This is a time-critical emergency. Do not delay appropriate empiric treatment for unnecessary tests.
simulationScript: Symptoms began today; photophobia and vomiting.
Examiner findings: T 39.3°C, GCS 13, neck stiffness; non-blanching rash may be provided if candidate asks about skin.
examinerInstructions: Allow the candidate to proceed without coaching.
If a required datum is not obtainable by simulation, provide it only when the candidate asks appropriately.
Award prompted checklist items no more than 1/2. Prioritise safe recognition, escalation and infection-control behaviour.
keyAnswerGuide: Suspected acute meningitis/meningococcal disease.
ABCDE, isolation precautions as appropriate, blood cultures/labs and immediate empiric IV antimicrobials according to age/local policy; adjunctive dexamethasone when indicated by protocol.
Lumbar puncture if safe and not contraindicated; do not delay antibiotics for CT/LP in a deteriorating patient.
suggestedApproach: Recognise → ABC → infection control → cultures → immediate antibiotics ± dexamethasone → LP when safe → notify/prophylaxis contacts if meningococcal.

checklist.criterion: Recognises meningitis and assesses ABC/GCS.
Checks rash and sepsis/shock features.
Uses appropriate droplet/infection-control precautions.
Obtains blood cultures and baseline labs without delaying therapy.
Starts immediate empiric IV antibiotics per current local guideline.
Considers dexamethasone when indicated.
Assesses contraindications to LP.
Performs/plans LP with CSF studies when safe.
Does not delay treatment for CT/LP in an unstable patient.
Escalates urgently and considers public-health/contact prophylaxis if meningococcal disease.

stations.scoringAnchor: Scoring anchor: 2 = complete/independent; 1 = partial or prompted; 0 = omitted/unsafe/incorrect. Prompted items score a maximum of 1/2.
promptQuestions: Name contraindications to immediate LP.
What CSF pattern suggests bacterial meningitis?
criticalSafetyErrors: Delaying antibiotics for CT or LP in a critically ill patient.
Performing LP despite clear contraindications.
sourceNote: Added high-yield station; meningitis is a core infection emergency and appears across KMU neuroscience/infection teaching.

stations.title: Pulmonary Tuberculosis
stations.primaryCompetency: Focused respiratory infection history, testing and infection control
candidateInstructions: Mr. Farhan Yousaf, 43, has cough for 5 weeks, weight loss, night sweats and intermittent haemoptysis.
Take a focused history, state investigations and explain immediate infection-control and referral steps.
candidateHandout: Think TB in chronic cough with constitutional symptoms and epidemiologic risk.
simulationScript: Lives with extended family; one relative was treated for TB last year.
No prior TB treatment.
examinerInstructions: Allow the candidate to proceed without coaching.
If a required datum is not obtainable by simulation, provide it only when the candidate asks appropriately.
Award prompted checklist items no more than 1/2. Prioritise safe recognition, escalation and infection-control behaviour.
keyAnswerGuide: Suspected pulmonary TB.
